title: Why surgery wasn’t an option to save Fiona the hippo | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Fiona the hippocaptured hearts around the world as a premature calf fighting for survival. Years later, fans who watched her grow are mourning her death after veterinarians were left without options to help her recover from ingesting a hat that accidentally landed in her habitat.

“We are in shock at the moment,” said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike in anews releaseThursday. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore.”

Born at a record-low preemie weight of 29 pounds, Fiona could barely walk and was unable to stand long enough to nurse from her mother. Her keepers formed “Team Fiona,” a round-the-clock feeding and care team to help the baby animal surviveagainst the odds,to the elation of her adoring fans worldwide.

Nearly 10 years later, the beloved hippo ingested a knit cap that entered her habitat by accident. The cap had been tossed into the air in front of the habitat and caught by a ceiling fan, which catapulted it through a 1-foot opening above the 12-foot-tall viewing windows, according to zoo communications director Michelle Curley.

As veterinarians considered their options, they determined a long open surgical incision for a hippo of Fiona’s size “would’ve been a death sentence,” the zoo added in asocial media video statement, saying veterinarians provided supportive care in hopes she would pass the hat.

Common hippos have unusually thick skin that, while designed to insulate their bodies and offer protection, can make it difficult for surgical incisions to heal, Zoo Miami associate veterinarian and hippo expert Dr. Gabriella Flacke, who consulted on Fiona’s case, told CNN.

Fiona died about two weeks after eating the hat. A necropsy done by the zoo revealed the hat was in the middle of Fiona’s small intestine, located 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines, according to a Fridaynews releaseby the zoo.

“Upper and lower GI endoscopy were unable to reach the object,” Cincinnati Zoo’s Director of Animal Health Dr. Mike Wenninger said in the release. “No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked.”

Fiona’s deathhas sparked an outpouring of grief across social media, with fans whowatched the hippo grow upexpressing their grief and frustration over the tragic events leading to her death.

“We have received so much love from our community and beyond,” Jenike said Friday. “We were touched when we saw stadiums, bridges, and buildings lit in purple last night. The support that we’re feeling from all over the world reminds me of the time when everyone pulled together to root for her to survive. She did, and she gave us almost a decade of smiles.”

“Fiona, you showed the world love,” one commenter wrote onthe zoo’s Facebook post about Fiona’s death. “Actions have consequences. The world is a dimmer place today.”

“This is an opportunity to remind ourselves and others that some actions can have really serious unintended consequences. Encouraging kids (as well as adults) to be mindful of their environment and their actions is so important in this and so many other situations,” another commenter wrote.

One of the people who knew Fiona best said she had lost someone special.

“Not only does it feel like I’ve lost a family member, friend and the most special, life changing animal I’ve ever worked with, but it also feels like I’ve lost part of my identity,” Jenna Wingate, Fiona’s primary keeper at the zoo, wrote in an Instagram tribute post. “It has always felt like we grew up together and I often used to smile thinking about growing old with her and her still being around when I would retire.”

Wingate said Fiona’s image is “all over” the pictures hanging in her home, the coffee mugs in her cabinet and the T-shirts in her dresser. “Not that we would or could ever forget her, but I’m not sure how we will find relief from the reminders of her anywhere we go.”

“She was magic wrapped in a hippo,” Wingate said.

Among those mourning Fiona was Timothy, a hippopotamus at the San Antonio Zoo who had spent years courting her from more than 1,000 miles away. Their long-distance romance began in 2018, when Timothy sent Fiona his first love letter. The pair exchanged letters and gifts over the years, with Timothy even arranging a mariachi serenade for her birthday.

The San Antonio Zoo also shared a goodbye to Fiona on behalf of Timothy, capturing the connection the two hippos had shared for years. In a farewell letter written from Timothy’s perspective, the zoo recalled their relationship, which developed with the help of the two animals’ care teams.

In the letter, Timothy called Fiona the most beautiful hippopotamus he had ever seen and remembered how her story inspired millions. Though the two never met nose to nose, the letter reads, she would “forever be with me.”

His farewell ended with a declaration that their romance would never be forgotten — and a message Fiona’s fans might find especially moving: “I may never have said ‘I love you,’ but please know I did. We all did.”

The story of the two hippos’ romance was sparked by a suggestion from Cincinnati Zoo docents, who brought a book about Fiona to San Antonio and wrote that she and Timothy would make a great couple, said Tim Morrow, president and CEO of the San Antonio Zoo.

The relationship soon captured the imagination of people well beyond the two zoos, Morrow told CNN’s Fredricka Whitfield.

“The world grasped on to the hopes of this relationship, and that someday these two hippos would be together, maybe start a family together,” Morrow said.

Visitors arriving at the zoo Thursday evening also took time to reflect on the beloved hippo’s life and impact. “Fiona fought a lot of obstacles in her life, as we all know, and that just showed a lot of character for her, and she truly was the queen of Cincinnati and the nation,” Debby Manningtold CNN affiliate WKRC, noting the whole mood in the zoo was somber.

“You come to the zoo, and it’s a special place,” visitor Chris Dalton told WKRC. “Fiona’s origins of sort of struggling at the beginning of her life, I think inspired a lot of people, particularly after Harambe.”

Harambe, a 17-year-old western lowland gorilla, was killed at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2016 in an attempt by the zoo to save a boy who slipped into the animal’s enclosure. The internet erupted with outrage and cries of “justice for Harambe” after the incident.

People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals was critical at the time and said the tragic episode was the latest proof that “captivity is never acceptable for gorillas or other primates.”The zoo defended its safety barriers, noting its regular inspections by the Association of Zoos & Aquariums and the United States Department of Agriculture, and strict adherence to safety guidelines.

Morrow believes Fiona’s story underscores the powerful connections people can form with animals, a bond he said can inspire greater interest in protecting them.

He hopes Timothy can help carry her legacy forward, keeping her story alive while encouraging people to learn more about hippos and the threats facing them.

Morrow also expressed sympathy for Fiona’s Cincinnati caretakers, many of whom had been with her since birth. Zoo employees often spend more time with the animals in their care than with their own families, he said, making the loss deeply personal.

“The passion of zoological professionals is unmatched,” Morrow said.

It is not uncommon for animals in zoos, particularly hippopotamuses, to die from ingesting foreign objects, Flacke told CNN.

“I’m aware of at least a dozen or more other cases in zoos around the world, not just in the US, that they’ve found their hippo is sick all of a sudden, they don’t know why, it passes away, and then when they do the autopsy or the necropsy, they find an intestinal obstruction, with a ball or with a children’s toy or something,” Flacke said.

When something splashes in the water, for any aquatic animal, like a hippo or an alligator, they are likely to check it out, often ingesting the object, Flacke explained.

The issue lies within the way zoos are designed for interaction with the animals, Flacke said. “You want to go there. You want to feel close to them. But then that makes it possible for things to fall in or things to get thrown in, whether that’s happening on purpose or not,” she said. “It’s an unfortunate reality.”

“While Fiona’s case was the result of a terrible accident, I think it’s important to remember that simple steps, like securing personal belongings around animal habitats, respecting safety barriers, and keeping potentially dangerous objects out of reach, can go a long way to keep animals safe,” American Veterinary Medical Association President Dr. Jennifer Quammen told CNN.

“We all share a responsibility to help protect animals from potentially dangerous objects. Something that seems harmless to us can have devastating consequences for an animal,” she added.

Accredited zoos build “empathy for the natural world” by connecting visitors with animals “that few will otherwise ever experience,” Melissa Howerton, executive vice president for the Association of Zoos & Aquariums, said, calling Fiona’s death a “tragic and unusual accident.”

“The bond Fiona had with so many around the world is an example of the impact animals have on people,” Howerton said. “Our hearts go out to the entire Cincinnati Zoo team and the community of animal lovers around the world who witnessed the wonder Fiona brought to everyone who saw her.”

While the Cincinnati Zoo remains open, the hippo habitat called Hippo Cove will be closed through the weekend to give the animal care team the space they need, the zoo said.

The other hippos, Fiona’s mother Bibi, her half-brother Fritz and other male Tucker, are eating and behaving normally, Cincinnati Zoo’s Director of Animal Care Christina Gorsuch said. “It’s difficult to know how they’re feeling, but they appear to be their normal selves.”

CNN’s Alaa Elassar contributed to this report.

CNN’s Alaa Elassar contributed to this report.
